name: Intestinal Behcet Disease

prevalence.estimate: 3-50% of Behcet disease patients (BD prevalence varies: 1/10,000 in Turkey to 1/300,000 in Western countries)

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: International Study Group Criteria for Behcet Disease with GI Involvement

criteria.description: Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers (>= 3 episodes in 12 months)
Typical intestinal ulcerations (deep, oval/round, discrete ulcers, often in ileocecal region)
Skin lesions (erythema nodosum, papulopustular lesions, pseudofolliculitis)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Recurrent oral ulceration plus characteristic intestinal ulcerations on endoscopy, in the context of other Behcet manifestations. Must exclude Crohn's disease and other causes of intestinal ulceration.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Intestinal involvement occurs in 3-25% of Behcet patients (higher in East Asia). Ileocecal region is most commonly affected. Deep ulcers carry perforation risk.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically round/oval, deep, discrete ulcers with sharp borders in ileocecal region

rare.notes: Life-threatening; deep ulcers penetrating through bowel wall

laboratory: Elevated ESR and CRP during flares
No specific serologic marker (unlike IBD: p-ANCA/ASCA typically negative)
Positive pathergy test in ~50% (more common in Middle Eastern/Asian patients)
imaging: CT enterography: mural thickening, ulcerations predominantly in ileocecal region
CT may show complications: perforation, fistula, abscess
genetic: HLA-B51 is strongest genetic risk factor
IL-10, IL-23R, ERAP1 gene polymorphisms associated
other: Colonoscopy: deep, round/oval, well-demarcated ulcers (fewer in number than Crohn's, with less cobblestoning)
Pathergy test: papular/pustular response at needle prick site at 24-48 hours
Biopsy: nonspecific inflammation; vasculitis may be seen but not always

distinguishingFeatures: Crohn's has longitudinal ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions throughout GI tract
Crohn's more commonly has ASCA positivity
Crohn's has granulomas on biopsy; Behcet typically does not
Behcet has oral/genital ulcers and uveitis
TB has transverse ulcers, caseating granulomas
NSAID ulcers resolve with drug withdrawal

redFlags: Severe visual changes suggesting posterior uveitis (risk of blindness)
Deep venous thrombosis or arterial aneurysm (vascular Behcet)
references: Hatemi G, et al. Behcet's syndrome: a critical digest of the recent literature. Clin Exp Rheumatol. 2017;35(108):3-14.
Cheon JH, et al. Development, validation, and responsiveness of a novel disease activity index for intestinal Behcet's disease. Inflamm Bowel Dis. 2011;17(2):605-613.
Yazici H, et al. Behcet syndrome: a contemporary view. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2018;4:18039.
